newsitem.title: USA: U.S. in frantic effort to end West Bank clashes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. in frantic effort to end West Bank clashes.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday mounted a frantic diplomatic effort to defuse a bloody Israel-Palestinian confrontation and urged both sides not to raise new issues that could scuttle fragile peace talks.
U.S. officials were reported to be in constant touch -- making several phone calls an hour -- with the region into Wednesday night.

Secretary of State Warren Christopher telephoned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Paris and other senior U.S. officials spoke to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat as well as senior Israeli and Egyptian leaders.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Christopher and Netanyahu "agreed that specific steps had to be taken to calm the situation. The prime minister told the secretary that he did have some ideas that he was going to put into play."
Burns said he believed Netanyahu intended to leave Paris as soon as he could after official appointments on Thursday morning and return to Israel, cutting short a European trip.
Later Christopher expressed "deep concern" over the bloody clashes in the West Bank and called on the two sides to return to the negotiating table.
Christopher, in New York for the U.N. General Assembly, said he urged Netanyahu to calm the situation and officials said U.S. Middle East Coordinator Dennis Ross passed the same message to Arafat.
"We've been following the situation last night and today with deep concern," Christopher told reporters before a meeting with Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen.

"We have urged the parties to defuse the situation, to restore calm in the area -- that's what needs to be done now. They should return to the negotiating table and make progress on the significant issues before them," he added.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry, with President Bill Clinton on a campaign trip in Philadelphia, said: "A return to violence and bloodshed is certainly not the way to deepen and nurture the peace process that has brought so much hope to both Arab and Jew."

U.S. officials spoke after Israeli soldiers were reported to have shot to death at least seven Palestinians, wounded 300 others and fought running gun battles with Arafat's police in the town of Ramallah, north of Bethlehem.
They were the bloodiest clashes in the West Bank since Palestinian rule began two years ago.
The fighting began after Netanyahu opened a second entrance to a tunnel in Jerusalem near the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa mosque, Islam's third-holiest shrine.
Netanyahu said he merely implemented a previous Labour government decision because the new tunnel made an important archaeological site more accessible to tourists.
The underground tunnel, with sensitivities for the whole Moslem world, provided a perfect vehicle to mobilise popular sentiment against Netanyahu's delay in implementing self-rule.
Palestinians say Israel is trying to turn Jerusalem into a wholly Jewish city, letting Jews build there but not Arabs.
Burns, in New York with Christopher, said: "The United States firmly believes that neither Israel nor the Palestinians should create other issues that can make the situation more difficult."
U.S. officials tried not to get involved in the specifics of the tunnel dispute.

But Burns said the clashes partly concerned "Jerusalem issues, religious issues, historical issues. The final status talks that have been agreed upon are the venue for those issues to be discussed, and our very strong view is that these issues will not be resolved on the street by either side."

Jerusalem's future is a key issue to be decided in final status peace talks agreed to by Israel and the Palestinians as part of their 1993 Oslo peace accords which provided for Palestinian self-rule in the West Bank and Gaza.
